title: The 4-Hour Battle That Made Every Navy Obsolete

scenes.text: It's nine p.m. on March 8th, 1862, and a warship is burning in front of you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: She is the USS Congress: fifty guns, and this morning she was the pride of the fleet.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: One enemy ship did this, in a single afternoon.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It destroyed two warships and killed more than two hundred and forty men.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Every cannonball the fleet fired at it just bounced off.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Tomorrow morning, it comes back to finish the job.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The only thing in its way is you: Lieutenant Samuel Dana Greene, age twenty-two.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Your ship is brand new, and it almost sank yesterday.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: By the end, you'll know how four hours tomorrow make every navy on Earth obsolete.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But first: how does one ship beat a whole fleet?
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Go back one year, to the navy yard at Norfolk, Virginia.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The Confederacy has almost no navy.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But it does have the burned hull of a Union frigate: the Merrimack.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So engineers cut her down to the waterline, and build an iron barn on top.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The walls are four inches of iron, over two feet of wood.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And the walls slope.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So a cannonball doesn't punch through: it skips off, like a stone off a pond.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: They rename her the CSS Virginia, and bolt an iron ram to her bow.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: She is slow, she leaks, and she needs half an hour to turn around.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: None of that matters, if nothing can hurt you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: March 8th, 1862. The Virginia steams out toward the Union's wooden fleet.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: On the USS Cumberland, the gunners fire broadside after broadside.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The shots ring off the iron, and fly into the sky.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The Virginia doesn't slow down. She rams the Cumberland below the waterline.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The Cumberland goes down with her flag still flying, and her guns still firing.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Next, the Congress runs aground, surrenders, and is set on fire.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It stays the US Navy's worst day for almost eighty years, until Pearl Harbor.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: In Washington, the Secretary of War keeps walking to the window.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He expects the Virginia to steam up the river and shell the White House.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: She can't. She sits far too deep in the water.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: But nobody in that room knows it.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The Union's answer comes from a Swedish-born engineer in New York: John Ericsson.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: His design has no masts, no sails, and almost no ship.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It is a flat iron raft, with one spinning iron tower in the middle.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: IRON RAFT + ONE SPINNING GUN TOWER

scenes.text: Two giant guns sit in a turret that turns to aim, so the ship doesn't have to.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The Navy is not convinced: if it fails, Ericsson must pay back every dollar.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He builds it in about a hundred days.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: People call it a cheesebox on a raft. Its real name is the USS Monitor.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You run the turret, and the whole crew is fifty-eight volunteers.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: On the way south, a storm nearly sinks you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Water pours in under the turret, and fumes knock out the engineers.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: You arrive one day late.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Which brings you back to the burning Congress. After midnight, she explodes.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Sunday morning. The Virginia comes back for a stranded Union frigate, the Minnesota.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Instead, she finds a cheesebox in the way.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Inside the turret, you pull the firing cord yourself.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: A solid iron ball, eleven inches wide, hits the Virginia.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It dents her. That's all.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Her shells hit your turret. They dent it. That's all.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: For about four hours the two ships circle, sometimes close enough to touch.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So why can't either one win? Two reasons, and both are a little embarrassing.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Reason one: your guns are a new size, and the Navy is afraid they will burst.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So you are ordered to load only half the gunpowder.
scenes.speaker: narrator

paper.text: ORDER: 15 POUNDS OF POWDER PER SHOT

scenes.text: Later tests show the guns could take double. Today, you'll never know.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Reason two: the Virginia came here to kill wooden ships.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So she carries exploding shells, and none of the solid shot that breaks iron.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Both ships brought the wrong ammunition to the first ironclad duel in history.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: One Confederate officer stops firing altogether.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He says he'd do as much damage by snapping his thumb at you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Meanwhile, the speaking tube to your captain breaks.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So his orders arrive on foot, carried by the paymaster and a clerk.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: It works about as well as it sounds.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And the turret is so hard to stop that you fire while it is still spinning.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Then, around noon, a shell bursts against the slit your captain is looking through.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Lieutenant John Worden is blinded. He hands the ship to you.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: By the time you steer back into the fight, the Virginia is leaving.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: She is leaking, the tide is falling, and she heads home to Norfolk.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Nobody has died today. Both sides announce that they won.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Told that the Minnesota is saved, Worden answers: then I can die happy.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: He doesn't. He lives another thirty-five years, and retires an admiral.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The real damage lands three thousand miles away, in London.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The Times counts a hundred and forty-nine first-class warships in the Royal Navy. After this fight, it says, there are two.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Every wooden warship on Earth has just become a target.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The Union alone orders dozens of copies, and calls every one a monitor.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The two originals don't survive the year.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The Virginia is blown up by her own crew in May, to keep her from capture.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: The Monitor sinks in a storm off Cape Hatteras on New Year's Eve, with sixteen men.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: Her turret was raised in 2002. You can stand next to it today, in Newport News, Virginia.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: And nearly every big-gun warship built since carries the same idea: a gun that turns.
scenes.speaker: narrator

scenes.text: So who really won, if neither ship could hurt the other? Tell me below.
scenes.speaker: narrator
scenes.title: THE 4 HOURS THAT MADE EVERY NAVY OBSOLETE

titleOptions: Why Two Ships That Couldn't Hurt Each Other Changed War Forever
The Day Wooden Warships Died (Hampton Roads, 1862)
Monitor vs. Virginia: The Draw That Sank Every Navy
meta.thumbnail: The round Monitor turret and the sloped Virginia casemate firing point-blank, cannonballs bouncing off both; text: 'NOBODY WON'
meta.description:
On March 8, 1862, one Confederate ironclad wrecked a Union fleet in an afternoon. The next morning it met a ship built in about 100 days, and the four-hour draw that followed made every wooden navy obsolete.

A comedic dramatization of documented history.

Sources:
S. Dana Greene, 'In the Monitor Turret', The Century Magazine (March 1885)
Naval History and Heritage Command, Battle of Hampton Roads - https://www.history.navy.mil
The Mariners' Museum and Park, USS Monitor Center - https://www.marinersmuseum.org
NOAA Monitor National Marine Sanctuary - https://monitor.noaa.gov
Diary of Gideon Welles (1911)
The Times (London), March 1862
factCheck: Monitor reached Hampton Roads about 9 p.m. on 8 March 1862; USS Congress (rated 50 guns) was burning and exploded after midnight (Greene 1885; NHHC)
8 March: CSS Virginia rammed and sank USS Cumberland (24 guns) and destroyed USS Congress; Union dead about 240-260 depending on the count (NHHC)
'Worst day until Pearl Harbor' is the common description of 8 March 1862 in US Navy histories; it is a characterisation, not a statistic
S. Dana Greene born 11 Feb 1840, executive officer of USS Monitor, age 22, fired the turret guns himself until Worden was wounded (Greene 1885)

CSS Virginia built on the burned hull of USS Merrimack at Gosport Navy Yard, Norfolk: casemate of 4 in. iron (two 2-in. layers) over about 24 in. of wood, sloped about 36 degrees, iron ram; took 30-40 minutes to turn

Stanton's fear that Virginia would come up the Potomac is from Gideon Welles's diary; the cabinet meeting was on the morning of 9 March (the script places it loosely after the 8 March disaster); Virginia drew about 22 ft, too deep for the river

USS Monitor: designed by John Ericsson (born in Sweden), contract 4 Oct 1861 for $275,000 with a refund clause, launched 30 Jan 1862 (about 100 days after the keel was laid), two 11-inch Dahlgren guns in a revolving turret, crew of 58 volunteers
'Cheesebox on a raft' was a contemporary nickname
Storm on the tow south, 7 March 1862: water entered under the turret and through the blower pipes; engineers overcome by fumes (Greene 1885)
9 March 1862: the duel lasted about four hours; nobody was killed on either ship
Monitor was limited to 15-lb powder charges; later tests allowed 30 lb. Whether full charges would have pierced Virginia is a common but unproven claim, so the script only says 'you'll never know'
Virginia carried mainly explosive shell, not armor-piercing solid shot, on 9 March
Lt. John Eggleston of Virginia reported he could do as much damage 'by snapping my thumb at her every two minutes and a half' (paraphrased in the script)
Speaking tube failed; orders were carried by paymaster William Keeler and captain's clerk Daniel Toffey; Greene fired 'on the fly' (Greene 1885)

Worden was blinded by a shell on the pilot house about noon (the script shows him in the turret for staging; he was in the pilot house); 'Then I can die happy' is from Greene 1885; Worden died in 1897 as a retired rear admiral
The Times (London): 'Whereas we had available for immediate purposes 149 first-class war-ships, we have now two'
Virginia destroyed by her crew 11 May 1862; Monitor foundered off Cape Hatteras 31 Dec 1862 with 16 men lost; turret raised 2002, displayed at The Mariners' Museum, Newport News
The Union ordered several dozen monitor-type ironclads during the war
